newsitem.title: USA: Solv-Ex raises $13 mln, project progresses.
newsitem.headline: Solv-Ex raises $13 mln, project progresses.

text.p: Solv-Ex Corp said it placed $13 million in debt to boost company coffers to $30 million as construction of the company's plant in Alberta to extract bitumen to produce crude oil and alumina wsa almost completed.
"We should have completed the construction by the end of the year," Solv-Ex's chairman and chief executive, John Rendall told Reuters.
The $13 million in debt is convertible into shares, and matures on November 30, 1998. The financing was closed on November 15.
Solv-Ex's president, Jack Butler said he was aware of concerns about the potential dilutive effect of such financing activities.

"We believe this is overshadowed by the potential benefits to be derived by proving the viability of our advanced technology and transforming this technology into profitable operations," Butler said in a press statement.

Rendall expected production at the Athabasca oil sands Bitumount Lease of bitumen blend (heavy oil) to start in the first quarter at the rate of 100,000 barrels per month, rising to 400,000 barrels by mid-year, and sold in the form of pipelineable crude oil from the fourth quarter.
Initial cash flow in 1997 will be $4 to $5 million per month, rising to $10 million per month by the year end, Rendall said.
"We have buyers who are buying it at the moment at about $13 per barrel, and our production costs are $5 per barrel," Rendall said.
Solv-Ex has spent $60 million on its project so far this year, and will spend some $80 million next year. Cash flow was projected at $10 million a month by the end of 1997.
Rendall said Solv-Ex will then try to raise that dramatically to a turnover of $200 million for 1998 as a whole.
The project, especially the aluminum aspect, has provoked some skepticism.

From the third quarter of 1997 Solv-Ex will sell 4,000 tonnes per month of what it calls titanium dioxide substitute for used in papermaking. Rendall said the price forecast for the product, a by-product from oil output, was $750 per tonne.

Solv-Ex said its benchscale aluminum production cell was running continuously and a pilot aluminum smelter would be built next year. It will use alumina obtained from the oil sands with the aim of producing aluminum at the rate of 25,000 tonnes a year from 1998.
The company has said aluminum would be produced at less than $500 per tonne.
Rendall declined to comment whether any aluminum company has approached Solv-Ex regarding the technology being used.
Deutsche Bank has the right to market Solv-Ex's aluminum technology in Europe, but Rendall was unable to say if the German company has been approached by potential users of the technology.
